headline: Hartford schools audit finds no fraud but exposes deep weaknesses in budgeting and oversight
dek: A state-ordered review did not find evidence of misappropriation, but auditors said missing records, turnover and opaque budget practices limited what they could determine about the district’s recurring deficits.
body: A forensic audit of Hartford Public Schools found no evidence of fraud or misappropriation, but it also found that the district’s financial systems were too inconsistent and incomplete to give leaders a clear account of how recurring budget problems developed. The Connecticut State Department of Education released the review Wednesday after CliftonLarsonAllen LLP presented its findings to the State Board of Education.

The result is not a clean bill of financial health. The audit examined the district’s fiscal years 2024 and 2025 and found weaknesses in budgeting, financial reporting, record retention, governance and internal controls. Auditors said those conditions reduced transparency and limited their ability to determine the precise causes and magnitude of some variances and deficits. [The Connecticut education department’s release](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/press-room/press-releases/2026/state-releases-hartford-public-schools-fiscal-years-2024-and-2025-forensic-audit-report) links to the full report and describes the review’s limits.

CliftonLarsonAllen said it used available financial records, system data, supporting documents and interviews, but could not fully reconstruct all financial activity from the two years. The firm cited significant turnover among district leaders and finance personnel, inconsistent historical records, incomplete email productions and other documentation gaps. Those limitations matter because they prevent the audit from answering every question about individual transactions or assigning a single, definitive cause to the district’s financial difficulties.

The report identified 14 key observations. Among them, budget transfers and expenditure reclassifications were used frequently to address account-level deficits, making it harder to see the operating reasons behind budget changes. Some costs were recorded in accounts that did not accurately describe their nature, while public budget materials, MUNIS data and other reports did not always present comparable information. The auditors said revised budgets shown to the board did not consistently make clear how spending compared with the originally approved budget.

The audit also pointed to management and oversight problems. Department leaders reported limited involvement in final budget decisions and limited access to current financial information. Board members generally understood their responsibility to approve the budget and monitor district finances, the report said, but their understanding of transfer requirements, finance committee duties and related policies was not consistent. The findings describe control weaknesses, not proof that any particular official acted improperly.

Other observations involved grants, purchasing and employee and vendor records. Grant-funded programs were not always separated clearly from ordinary operating activity or reassessed when grant support ended. Procurement documentation was not always readily available at the transaction level. Auditors also found duplicate contact information in employee and vendor records and matches between active employees and vendors who received payments. CliftonLarsonAllen said those matches do not by themselves indicate fraud or improper relationships, but they should be reviewed for legitimate explanations, disclosures and compliance with conflict-of-interest and procurement rules.

The findings arrive after Hartford schools reported a projected multimillion-dollar shortfall and state officials expanded their intervention. NBC Connecticut reported that the State Board ordered the audit after the district reported a deficit of about $29 million for the 2026-27 school year. [NBC’s report](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/no-misuse-of-funds-found-in-hartford-public-schools-forensic-audit/3782798/) also noted the distinction between the absence of identified misuse and the continuing budget problems. WFSB reported that auditors could not fully review some activity because records were missing or incomplete and that special education, transportation and lost grant funding were among the district’s major cost pressures. [Its Oct. 8 report](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/08/hartford-schools-audit-finds-no-fraud-cites-financial-oversight-weaknesses/) said the recommendations call for better expense tracking, stronger board oversight and tighter record-keeping.

CliftonLarsonAllen issued 33 recommendations for the district and eight more for the Board of Education. The state says implementing them would improve transparency, accountability and financial stewardship. The review is not finished: fiscal year 2026 information was not sufficiently final for definitive findings, and the auditors will begin that work after Hartford completes its year-end closeout. For families, employees and taxpayers, that next phase will be important because the newly released audit identifies why the district’s records were difficult to trust without yet resolving the full scale or origin of the latest deficit.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Hartford schools audit finds no fraud, cites financial weaknesses
seoDescription: A Connecticut-ordered audit found no evidence of fraud in Hartford schools but cited weaknesses in budgeting, records, governance and oversight.
